headline_en: 72 percent of workers who went abroad on 'free visas' took loans to do so
summary_en: A survey by the migrant organisation OKUP of 1,084 households of workers who went to Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, the UAE and Saudi Arabia in 2022 found that workers going on so-called 'free visas' (no guaranteed job) paid about five times the government-set cost, 72 percent borrowed, and 43 percent got no work on arrival. Many had to pay again in the destination for a work permit (iqama), 4 percent came home at their own cost and 14 percent stayed on undocumented. The findings were discussed at a Dhaka hotel on Sunday 19 October 2025, where the expatriates' welfare secretary and BMET's additional director general spoke.

facts.date: 2022 departures; data collected November 2023 to March 2024
facts.statement: OKUP (Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program) surveyed the households of 1,084 Bangladeshi workers who went to Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia in 2022; data were collected from November 2023 to March 2024 in eight districts: Bagerhat, Chattogram, Cumilla, Dhaka, Manikganj, Narsingdi, Satkhira and Sunamganj. The study is titled (in translation) 'An in-depth assessment of lost remittance: the impact of Bangladeshis' free visa migration on the macroeconomy'.

Under the so-called 'free visa', Bangladeshi workers go to Middle East countries year after year without any guarantee of a specific job; they are charged about five times the government-set cost and then have to spend more money after arrival to get a work permit.
The government-set average cost of going to Middle East countries from Bangladesh is BDT 116,224 (1 lakh 16 thousand 224 taka), according to the OKUP study presentation.
Workers who went to the Middle East in the name of a 'free visa' spent BDT 499,802 (4 lakh 99 thousand 802 taka), against a government-set average of BDT 116,224, according to the OKUP survey.
OKUP survey: 43 percent of the surveyed workers who went to the Gulf countries in 2022 did not get work on arrival; 57 percent got a work permit on arrival.
OKUP survey: 21 percent of the workers, finding no work on arrival, spent about a further 1.5 lakh taka to obtain a work permit (iqama); 4 percent got work after spending BDT 44,000.

OKUP survey: 4 percent of the workers returned to Bangladesh after finding no work, paying for the return themselves; 14 percent could not afford the extra cost, got no work permit, could not return and stayed on undocumented in the destination country.

OKUP survey: before going abroad the worker's average monthly income was BDT 9,000 and the family's income was BDT 36,238; the cost of going exceeded the family's annual income. 72 percent said they took a loan of some kind, 11 percent mortgaged land and 6 percent sold land; those who came back without a job could not recover the mortgaged land.
The OKUP survey states that 938,000 (9 lakh 38 thousand) workers went from Bangladesh to the Middle East in 2022.

OKUP survey: 51 percent of respondents (554 workers) went abroad knowing it was a 'free visa'. Of these, 54 percent went through illegal broker networks, 7 percent directly through a recruiting agency, 8 percent through a family member and 31 percent through a distant relative.
OKUP survey respondents were 91 percent men and 9 percent women; the article says women mainly go as domestic workers, for which the 'free visa' does not apply.

Md. Ashraf Hossain, additional director general of BMET and administrator of BAIRA, said there is no such thing as a 'free visa': under ILO convention a worker cannot be sent without an employment contract, yet for Saudi Arabia an employment contract is found for only 3-4 percent of workers.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Ashraf Hossain, additional director general, BMET

facts.statement: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry secretary Neyamat Ullah Bhuiyan said the government is working to keep every worker's recruitment transparent and accountable, takes a hard line against money laundering, and is stressing sending workers at the employer's cost through bilateral agreements.
facts.source_in_article: Neyamat Ullah Bhuiyan, secretary, expatriates' welfare ministry

facts.statement: OKUP chairperson Shakirul Islam said the recommendation is legal action: those involved in 'free visa' recruitment are never punished, the law exists but must be enforced, migration costs must be monitored and skills training prioritised.

named_actors.name: Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program (OKUP)
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Grassroots migrants' organisation that ran the free-visa survey; chairperson Shakirul Islam presented it, executive director Omar Faruque Chowdhury gave the welcome speech.

named_actors.name: Md. Ashraf Hossain
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Additional director general of BMET and administrator of BAIRA; said free visas do not exist and only 3-4 percent of Saudi-bound workers have an employment contract.

named_actors.name: Neyamat Ullah Bhuiyan
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Secretary of the Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry; spoke at the event.

headline_en: Greece toughens migration law, plans to send back some Bangladeshis this month
summary_en: Greece's parliament passed a law (about 3 September 2025) that toughens penalties for rejected asylum seekers and speeds up their return: undocumented migrants not entitled to asylum must be returned or detained for at least 24 months and fined up to 10,000 euros. Greece says it has returned hundreds of irregular migrants since suspending asylum applications in July and has planned return flights this month for some migrants from Pakistan, Bangladesh and Egypt. UNHCR and rights groups criticised the law and Greek pushbacks.

facts.statement: A law passed by Greece's parliament says undocumented migrants who enter the southernmost edge of Europe from a third country the EU considers safe and who are not entitled to asylum must be returned to their own country, or be detained for at least 24 months and pay a fine of up to 10,000 euros. The law toughens punishment for migrants whose applications are rejected and speeds up their return.

Greece said it has returned hundreds of irregular migrants since suspending asylum applications in July 2025, and that flights are planned in September 2025 to return some migrants from Pakistan, Bangladesh and Egypt.

After arrivals rose in 2025 via Libya to the Greek islands of Crete and Gavdos, the Greek government temporarily banned the processing of asylum applications from migrants arriving from North Africa (the suspension dates from July 2025).
In 2025 the number of migrants reaching Europe from Libya across the Mediterranean via the Greek islands of Crete and Gavdos rose; most arrivals in Greece that year came at its southern border.
Since coming to power in 2019, Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis's administration has built a fence on Greece's northern border and stepped up sea patrols to discourage migrants from crossing.

Greek migration minister Thanos Plevris told parliament that the rights of Greek citizens who want to protect Greece matter more than the rights of a person whose application has been rejected, because that person is staying in Greece illegally.

UNHCR said the new Greek law could expose migrants who need international protection to punishment and proposed a fast-track asylum procedure to quickly identify refugees and non-refugees. Rights groups accuse Athens of forcibly pushing migrants back at sea and land borders; the EU border agency said in 2025 it was reviewing 12 cases of possible rights violations by Greece.
facts.source_in_article: UNHCR; rights groups; EU border agency

facts.statement: In 2015-16 more than 1 million migrants from the Middle East and Africa entered Europe, a large share through Greece; arrivals in Greece fell after that until 2025.

named_actors.name: Thanos Plevris
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Greek migration minister who defended the tougher law in parliament.

headline_en: Reforming the Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry: separating welfare from employment
summary_en: An opinion piece by a Bangladeshi who has lived in Japan for about three decades argues that the Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry is really about sending workers, not welfare. The writer proposes setting up expatriate welfare wings in embassies alongside labour welfare wings, moving the ministry's three workforce bodies to the labour ministry, and merging the rest with the foreign ministry as India did in 2016. It gives figures on Bangladeshis in Japan, remittance sources and worker skill levels.

facts.statement: Bangladesh's Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry was formed in 2001; four bodies sit under it: the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET), Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL), the Wage Earners' Welfare Board and Probashi Kallyan Bank.

Bangladesh has 29 labour welfare wings in 27 countries under the Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry; no country has an 'expatriate welfare wing'. The total number of Bangladeshi expatriates worldwide has passed 1.25 crore.

Bangladesh Bank data: in the first four months of FY2024-25 the United States was the top remittance-sending country, followed by the UAE and Saudi Arabia; half of the country's remittance comes from the United States, European countries, Australia, Japan and South Korea, where people mostly go by their own efforts.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank data, cited by the writer

facts.statement: A 2019 Bangladesh Bank survey found that 62 percent of workers going abroad from Bangladesh were unskilled and 36 percent semi-skilled.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank survey 2019, cited by the writer

facts.statement: According to the writer, the number of Bangladeshis in Japan passed 50,000 by 2000, fell to 15,000 by about 2020 because most had to leave for lack of a skilled-worker quota visa, and has risen again to 25,000 under the Japan-Bangladesh strategic partnership; Nepalis in Japan were under 5,000 in 2000 and now exceed 2 lakh.
facts.source_in_article: the writer (resident in Japan for about three decades)

facts.statement: The weekly number of flights on Biman Bangladesh's Dhaka-Tokyo route, launched in 2023, has been reduced; the writer says the route survives on Nepali passengers.

The writer says several welfare and rehabilitation schemes for expatriates have been launched and are presented at events held by embassy labour welfare wings, but most expatriates do not know about them.
World Bank data: foreigners working in Bangladesh sent USD 137 million to their home countries in 2022; analysts believe the true figure is much higher because many lack a legal work permit.
facts.source_in_article: World Bank data, cited by the writer

facts.statement: India set up a ministry of overseas Indian affairs in 2004 and merged it with the foreign ministry in 2016; India's remittance was USD 69 billion in 2015 and USD 111 billion in 2022. Nepal and Sri Lanka have no separate overseas employment ministry; it is part of the labour ministry.

The writer proposes: set up expatriate welfare wings in embassies alongside labour welfare wings; move the ministry's three bodies that produce and supply skilled workers to the Ministry of Labour and Employment; and merge the expatriates' welfare ministry with the foreign ministry.

key_quote_bn: প্রবাসীদের জন্য বেশ কয়েকটি কল্যাণ ও পুনর্বাসনমূলক স্কিম চালু করা হলেও সে সম্পর্কে অধিকাংশ প্রবাসীই জানেন না।

headline_en: The rules that must be introduced for recruiting agencies sending workers abroad
summary_en: A column by North South University migration researchers asks the government to introduce a performance-based ranking system for Bangladeshi recruiting agencies, and to bring brokers under a policy. It lists proposed ranking criteria such as IOM's IRIS certification, publishing the full recruitment process and all costs in Bangla on the agency's website, quarterly reports audited by BMET, own job portals and training centres, worker satisfaction surveys at the airport, local offices, emergency help and BAIRA's involvement. It states no such ranking exists yet; these are proposals, not rules in force.

facts.statement: Researchers at North South University's Center for Migration Studies wrote that in most cases Bangladeshi migrants have to spend a lot of money because of brokers at various stages of recruitment and because of licensed recruiting agents, so that the bulk of what they earn abroad goes to pay off the migration cost; many fall into debt or are forced to sell all their property to pay it.
facts.source_in_article: the writers (Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza, K M Noor-E-Jannat, North South University)

facts.statement: The writers ask the Bangladesh government to set up a performance-based ranking system for recruiting agencies to bring transparency and accountability, and suggest that brokers also be brought under a policy; the column presents this as a proposal, meaning no such ranking was in place when it was written.

IOM's IRIS (International Recruitment Integrity System) certification is a model designed to ensure ethics and transparency in recruitment; the writers propose a certification scheme in Bangladesh based on it, with IRIS-certified recruiting agencies given priority in the ranking.

Proposed ranking criterion: whether a recruiting agency publishes on its own website, in Bangla, the full recruitment process and the full cost of migrating to each country, including the employment contract with the employer, agency fee, visa cost, medical cost, airfare and all other costs.

Proposed: licensed recruiting agencies should report all information, including how money received from recruitment fees was spent, to the authorities quarterly; BMET should audit the quarterly reports and agencies should publish BMET's review on their websites.

Other proposed ranking criteria for recruiting agencies: an own job portal with workers' CVs, employers' contracts, job advertisements and links to destination-country job portals; speed and low cost of arranging jobs and visas; an own training centre with pre-departure training in addition to BMET's and adequate food and lodging; a worker satisfaction survey taken at the airport before departure plus regular feedback from workers abroad; staffed district or upazila offices; regularly updated websites; an advisory committee with civil-society experts; MoUs with foreign firms or job portals; help rescuing workers in crisis and repatriating bodies after death; reintegration or jobs for returnees; and social activities.

The writers say BAIRA (Bangladesh Association of International Recruiting Agencies) must take an active part in a ranking system and monitor its implementation, and must first bring transparency to its own organisational structure.

key_quote_bn: নিয়োগকর্তার সঙ্গে অভিবাসনপ্রত্যাশী কর্মীদের কাজের চুক্তিনামা, এজেন্সির ফি, ভিসার খরচ, মেডিকেল খরচ, বিমানভাড়া ও অন্যান্য যাবতীয় খরচের বিবরণ ওয়েবসাইটে উন্মুক্ত রাখতে হবে।

headline_en: Expatriates will get VIP service at the airport: expatriates' welfare adviser
summary_en: At a press conference on Tuesday 24 September 2024, expatriates' welfare adviser Professor Asif Nazrul announced that VIP service for expatriates at the airport would start within a month, first for those arriving from the Middle East. He also announced remittance measures (loan instalments payable by remittance to Probashi Kallyan Bank, loans from 12 commercial banks pending a Bangladesh Bank guarantee, PKB booths in Sonali and Agrani branches, removal of the BDT 1 crore cap on Wage Earners' Bonds), an end to the ministry's recruitment-permission step, registration of brokers and category certificates for agencies. He said 25 percent of the 17,000 workers who could not go to Malaysia had got refunds, and that 57 Bangladeshis jailed in the UAE for protests had returned after a special pardon.

facts.date: announced 24 September 2024; to start within one month
facts.statement: Expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul said VIP service for expatriates would start at the airport within one month; in the first phase expatriates returning from the Middle East would get it. Expatriates would get all VIP facilities except the lounge and the special immigration desk.
facts.source_in_article: Asif Nazrul, expatriates' welfare and overseas employment adviser, press conference

facts.statement: Asif Nazrul said chief adviser Dr Muhammad Yunus's influence would be used to untangle the deadlock over the Malaysian labour market, and that news about expanding labour markets would be given within the next two months.

Asked about refunds for workers who could not go to Malaysia, Asif Nazrul said it had been confirmed that 25 percent of the 17,000 workers had got their money back, and that refunds for 100 percent of the workers would be ensured.
On the syndicate in the Malaysian labour market, Asif Nazrul said efforts are being made to break the syndicate and that the corruption would be investigated.

A list of 87 Bangladeshi expatriates who were arrested and jailed in various countries for demonstrating in support of the anti-discrimination movement and then returned home has been made; of them, 57 returned from the UAE after receiving a special pardon on the chief adviser's initiative. Asif Nazrul said steps had been taken to rehabilitate them and jobs would be arranged.
Expatriates can from now on pay their loan instalments by sending remittance directly to Probashi Kallyan Bank; this was not possible before.
Twelve commercial banks have agreed to give loan support to expatriates; it will start once Bangladesh Bank provides a credit guarantee.
In remote areas where Probashi Kallyan Bank has no branch, Probashi Kallyan Bank booths will be opened in branches of Sonali Bank and Agrani Bank.
The BDT 1 crore limit on buying Wage Earners' Bonds has been removed; expatriates can now buy bonds of any amount.

Sending a worker abroad needed permission from three bodies; from now on recruitment permission from the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry is no longer required, which the ministry says will cut workers' hassle and time.

The ministry said brokers (middlemen), who drive up migration cost, will be registered, and recruiting agencies will be given category certificates based on experience so that everyone can know an agency's standard.

The ministry said Bangladesh's embassies and labour wings abroad, about which there are various complaints, will be put under strict monitoring: they must regularly send the ministry reports of expatriates' complaints and the action taken, and officials who do not work will be reassigned.

named_actors.name: Asif Nazrul
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Adviser for expatriates' welfare and overseas employment; announced the airport VIP service, remittance measures and recruitment reforms.

key_quote_bn: বিদেশে কর্মী পাঠাতে তিনটি সংস্থার অনুমতি লাগে, এখন থেকে প্রবাসী কল্যাণ মন্ত্রণালয় থেকে আর নিয়োগ অনুমতি লাগবে না।

headline_en: Saudi government working to protect the rights of Bangladeshi and foreign workers
summary_en: A press release from the Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh reports a courtesy meeting and workshop on Wednesday 29 May 2024 between Saudi assistant deputy minister Faisal Al Dafayan of the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development and the embassy's deputy chief of mission Md. Abul Hasan Mridha. The Saudi side presented its digitalised services and said 1,200 labour inspectors had resolved about 1 million complaints in 2023; the embassy asked for cooperation on visas with guaranteed work and iqama, return of women workers at contract end, quick return of workers with expired iqamas, and settling complaints against Bangladeshi agencies in the Musaned system.

facts.statement: Saudi assistant deputy minister Faisal Al Dafayan of the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development said Bangladeshis are currently the largest group among foreign workers in Saudi Arabia and that demand for them in the Saudi labour market is rising.
facts.source_in_article: Faisal Al Dafayan, Saudi assistant deputy minister (embassy press release)

facts.statement: Faisal Al Dafayan said Saudi Arabia recently appointed 1,200 labour inspectors to act on workers' complaints, and that they resolved about 10 lakh (1 million) complaints in 2023.

The Saudi human resources ministry said it is automating the whole process including worker recruitment and asked the Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh to help familiarise Bangladeshi workers with its digitalised service systems; the workshop presented what the digital systems offer and how workers can use them. The article does not name the systems apart from Musaned.

Bangladesh embassy deputy chief of mission Md. Abul Hasan Mridha asked Saudi Arabia for cooperation on: issuing visas with assured work and iqama, sending women workers back at the end of their contracts, quick return home of workers whose iqama has expired, and settling complaints involving Bangladeshi recruiting agencies in the Musaned system.

The Bangladesh embassy asked the Saudi Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development to designate a focal point for immediate resolution of workers' problems, and assistant deputy minister Faisal Al Dafayan agreed.

named_actors.name: Faisal Al Dafayan
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Assistant deputy minister, Saudi Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development; presented Saudi labour measures to the Bangladesh embassy.

named_actors.name: Md. Abul Hasan Mridha
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Deputy chief of mission; raised Bangladeshi workers' issues. Also present: counsellor (labour) Muhammad Rezaye Rabbi, counsellor (political) Muhammad Humayun Kabir, first secretary (labour) Muhammad Alamgir Hossain, second secretary (press) Asaduzzaman Khan.

key_quote_bn: শ্রমিকদের অভিযোগ আমলে নিয়ে সমস্যা সমাধানে সম্প্রতি ১ হাজার ২০০ শ্রম পরিদর্শক নিয়োগ দেওয়া হয়েছে

headline_en: Take action against the fraud syndicate
summary_en: An editorial says the 2022 reopening of the Malaysian labour market benefited a Bangladesh-Malaysia syndicate rather than workers: the legal cost is BDT 80,000 but workers paid 4 to 4.5 lakh taka and most found no job. It reports that Malaysia has stopped approving new foreign-worker applications, with a 31 March 2024 visa-application deadline and 31 May 2024 as the last date of entry. It asks why no action is taken against the Bangladeshi side of the syndicate.

facts.statement: According to Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry sources, the Malaysian government is no longer approving any new applications to recruit foreign workers. Those who already have approval must submit visa applications by 31 March 2024, after which Malaysia will take no more worker visa applications; those who have or will get visas must enter Malaysia by 31 May 2024, after which no Bangladeshi can go there for a job.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry sources

facts.statement: By law it should cost a worker BDT 80,000 to go to Malaysia from Bangladesh, the editorial states.
Bangladeshis going to Malaysia had to pay 4 to 4.5 lakh taka (the editorial also cites Prothom Alo reporting of 4 to 5 lakh taka per worker), against a legal cost of BDT 80,000.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial, citing Prothom Alo reports

facts.statement: According to Prothom Alo reports, BDT 1.5 lakh had to be paid for each worker to the syndicate formed in the name of 100 agencies to send a worker to Malaysia, and the same syndicate then ran a business in the name of medical tests; many workers got no job on arrival.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo reports cited in the editorial

facts.statement: Most of those who recently went to Malaysia through the syndicate for large sums got no job and are living in inhuman conditions there, the editorial says.

Malaysia's labour market closed to Bangladesh from September 2018 over allegations that 10 Bangladeshi recruiting agencies formed a syndicate and engaged in corruption; it reopened in August 2022 after talks. The government first allowed 25 agencies to send workers and later raised the number to 100; the demand to open it to all agencies was not met.
Malaysia decided to suspend new recruitment as pressure on its government from international human rights organisations grew.
BMET data: 12.5 lakh Bangladeshi workers went to Malaysia legally from 1992 to January 2024; more than 3.5 lakh of them went in 2023 and 50,000 in 2022.

State minister for expatriates' welfare Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury said relations with Malaysia are good and worker sending will not be disrupted; Malaysian envoy Haznah Md. Hashim, after meeting foreign minister Hasan Mahmud, acknowledged 'syndicates at both ends'.
The editorial says no action has been taken against the Bangladeshi syndicate members, including those whose fraud led to the pre-2018 closure of the Malaysian market.

named_actors.name: Syndicate of 100 Bangladeshi recruiting agencies (unnamed)
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Agencies permitted to send workers to Malaysia that, together with some Malaysian private agencies, resorted to fraud and took BDT 1.5 lakh per worker.
named_actors.status: no action taken as of March 2024, per the editorial

named_actors.name: Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury
named_actors.what_the_article_says: State minister for expatriates' welfare and overseas employment; said worker sending to Malaysia would not be disrupted.

key_quote_bn: যাঁরা ইতিমধ্যে ভিসা নিয়েছেন বা নেবেন; তাঁদের মালয়েশিয়ায় প্রবেশের শেষ সময় আগামী ৩১ মে।

headline_en: New blow to employment in Saudi Arabia after Houthi attack on airport
summary_en: After repeated attacks on Riyadh's King Khalid airport in October 2026 (the deadliest on Saturday 10 October killed 13 people including two Bangladeshis), flights from Dhaka to Saudi Arabia were cancelled or suspended: 61 flights and 8,381 passengers were affected according to the civil aviation authority. Workers on leave cannot return and fear losing visas and jobs, while BMET figures show clearances for Saudi Arabia in 2026 were already about 46 percent down on 2025. The article also gives figures on Bangladesh's dependence on a few markets, bodies of migrants returned, and Bangladeshis killed and injured in the Middle East war.

facts.statement: Amid the ongoing Middle East conflict, King Khalid airport in Riyadh was attacked for the fourth time in five days on Sunday (about 11 October 2026). The deadliest attack was on Saturday (about 10 October 2026), killing 13 people including two Bangladeshis; one injured Bangladeshi was in critical condition. Dhaka-Riyadh flights began to be cancelled after that. The headline attributes the attack to the Houthis.

A CAAB (Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh) press release late on 12 October 2026 said restrictions at various Saudi airports directly affected 61 flights of various airlines on direct and transit routes with Bangladesh, some cancelled and some suspended; 8,381 passengers who were due to fly from Dhaka to Saudi destinations were affected.

Per CAAB as printed, of the 61 affected flights 12 were direct Saudi flights and 'the remaining 39' transit flights; the article then lists affected direct flights as Biman Bangladesh Airlines 9, US-Bangla Airlines 2, Saudia 4 and Riyadh Airways 7. These figures do not add up to each other in the article.

Riyadh airport was declared closed until 3 am on the night of Monday 12 October 2026, with a fresh decision to follow. US-Bangla Airlines cancelled all its Dhaka-Riyadh-Dhaka flights until 21 October 2026; Biman suspended all Dhaka-to-Riyadh flights until 17 October 2026 and said passengers would be told the new schedule. Other airlines had not announced advance cancellations and were giving flight status daily.
facts.source_in_article: Biman and US-Bangla press releases; reporter

facts.statement: From 12 October 2026 some Dhaka flights to Jeddah were also cancelled, Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport said; the airport's flight information showed the 5:30 pm flynas flight to Jeddah as cancelled.

BAIRA members and BMET sources say that in 2026 on average 1,200 new workers a day went from Bangladesh to Saudi Arabia and 600 to 700 workers a day returned there after leave; on that basis about 5,500 workers were stuck by the flight disruption over three days.

Bangladesh embassy sources in Saudi Arabia said about 500 Bangladeshi passengers were stranded at Riyadh airport after the attack, including arrivals from Bangladesh, Umrah pilgrims and passengers waiting for domestic and international flights. The embassy, with the airport authority, Saudi immigration and the airlines, arranged accommodation, food and alternative travel; about 400 were arranged to fly home via King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, and two Bangladeshi workers on a Saudia flight from Riyadh to Bahrain were helped to cross to Bahrain by the Al Khobar land border.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh embassy sources in Saudi Arabia

facts.statement: Workers on leave in Bangladesh who cannot fly back face uncertainty over visa validity and jobs. Former BAIRA secretary general Ali Haider Chowdhury said many visas may expire, that visas of stranded people were renewed during the Kuwait war and the Covid pandemic, and that the government could talk to Saudi Arabia again. State minister Md. Nurul Haque said government-level talks would be held to arrange travel for those stuck, and that visa validity had been extended automatically earlier, at the start of the Middle East war.
facts.source_in_article: Ali Haider Chowdhury, former BAIRA secretary general; Md. Nurul Haque, state minister for expatriates' welfare

facts.statement: BMET figures: up to 12 October 2025, 853,066 people had taken clearance to go abroad; in the same period of 2026 the number was 580,632, about 32 percent lower. Clearances for Saudi Arabia alone fell from 572,054 to 311,567, about 46 percent lower.

BMET: in the first 12 days of October 2025, 14,174 people took BMET clearance for various countries, against 11,122 in the same days of 2026; for Saudi Arabia the figures were 3,971 in 2025 and 1,850 in 2026.

About 6.25 lakh Bangladeshis went to Saudi Arabia for work in 2024 and more than 755,000 in 2025; in the first nine months of 2026 about 309,000 went. BMET says more than 11.32 lakh workers went abroad in total in 2025.

Analysis of Expatriates' Welfare Ministry data: in the 15 years from January 2011 to December 2025 Bangladesh sent more than 1 crore 10 lakh workers to 203 countries; about 79 percent went to just five countries and 94 percent to 10 countries (Saudi Arabia, Oman, Qatar, UAE, Malaysia, Singapore, Kuwait, Jordan, Bahrain and Maldives). To 98 countries fewer than 100 workers were sent in the decade and a half.

summary_en: Sohag Munshi (24) of Rajoir, Madaripur, who left home on 23 September 2025 to reach Italy irregularly via Libya under a BDT 22 lakh deal with local brokers, died on 24 July 2026 in a brokers' detention site in Libya, his family says after torture. His mother has filed a written complaint at Rajoir police station; the main accused, Julhas Sardar, a listed top trafficker with at least 10 cases, was arrested a few days earlier and is in jail.

facts.statement: Sohag Munshi (24), son of Ashraf Ali Munshi of Majumdarkandi, Rajoir municipality, Madaripur, died on 24 July 2026 in a brokers' detention site in Libya while trying to reach Italy irregularly; his family alleges he died from torture by brokers. facts.statement: Sohag Munshi left home on 23 September 2025; he was first flown from Dhaka to Saudi Arabia, kept there a few days, then sent to Benghazi, Libya. On arrival in Benghazi, Bangladeshi brokers living in Libya took his passport and moved him to a detention site in Tripoli.

headline_en: Bangladeshi woman worker killed in Israeli attack in Lebanon
summary_en: Dipali Begum (34), a Bangladeshi woman worker from Charbhadrasan, Faridpur, was killed on Wednesday 8 April 2026 when an Israeli air strike collapsed her employer's house in the Hamra area of Beirut; seven people died including the employer and family members. She is the eighth Bangladeshi reported killed in the Middle East war that began on 28 February 2026 and the first in Lebanon. Her body is in the Rafik Hariri hospital morgue and officials say repatriation through diplomatic channels has begun.

facts.statement: Dipali Begum (34), daughter of Sheikh Mofazzal of Purba Shalepur Munshirchar village, Char Harirampur union, Charbhadrasan upazila, Faridpur, was killed on the evening of Wednesday 8 April 2026 when Israeli forces bombed her employer's (kafeel's) house in the Hamra area of Beirut and the building collapsed; seven people died including the employer and his family members. She had gone to Lebanon two years earlier.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh embassy in Beirut; a foreign ministry official

facts.statement: Dipali Begum's body is kept in the morgue of Rafik Hariri hospital in Beirut; the Bangladesh embassy said it is in contact with the hospital, and Charbhadrasan UNO Suraiya Momtaz said the process of bringing the body home quickly through diplomatic channels has begun.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh embassy in Beirut; UNO Suraiya Momtaz

facts.statement: About a month before her death Dipali Begum had moved with her employer's family from the Tyre area of Lebanon to Beirut seeking safety because fighting was heavier in Tyre; she was killed in Beirut.

Dipali Begum's is the eighth reported death of a Bangladeshi in the Middle East war between Iran and the United States and Israel, which began on 28 February 2026, and the first in Lebanon; in the 40 days of war seven Bangladeshis were killed in Saudi Arabia, Oman, Bahrain and Iraq.

Israel has been attacking Lebanon since the war began on 28 February 2026 and had not stopped as of 10 April 2026, although the United States and Iran announced a ceasefire on 8 April 2026; Bangladeshi workers in Lebanon are living in fear.
According to the migration research body RMMRU, there are about 1.5 lakh Bangladeshi workers in Lebanon, more than half of them women.
Dipali Begum's family in Faridpur learned of her death on the morning of Friday 10 April 2026 by a phone call from the owner of the shop through which she used to send money home.

headline_en: Lured by brokers, some willingly and some under pressure send their children abroad by illegal routes
summary_en: A rubber boat carrying 38 people left Libya for Greece on 21 March 2026, lost its way and drifted for six days; 18 people died of hunger and weakness and their bodies were thrown into the sea, 12 of them from Sunamganj (six from Derai, five from Jagannathpur, one from Dowarabazar). Survivors were rescued off Greece on Friday 27 March 2026. The article names local brokers in Sunamganj, reports payments of 10 to 20 lakh taka per person, and says police and the district administration are listing brokers and preparing cases.

facts.statement: A rubber boat with 38 people left Libya for Greece on 21 March 2026, lost its way in the Mediterranean and was at sea for six days; food ran out and 18 people died one by one of weakness. The bodies stayed on the boat for two days and were then thrown into the sea when they began to smell. The dead include 12 from Sunamganj: six from Derai upazila, five from Jagannathpur upazila and one from Dowarabazar upazila. The deaths became known after the others were rescued off the Greek coast on Friday 27 March 2026.

The family of Shayek Ahmad (23) of Tiargaon village, Raniganj union, Jagannathpur, Sunamganj paid a broker BDT 12 lakh in two instalments before his 'game' crossing from Libya to Greece; his father Akhlus Mia sold cattle and haor land to raise it. Shayek died in the Mediterranean.

Residents of Jagannathpur, Sunamganj say 10 to 20 lakh taka has to be paid per person to the local broker ring for the irregular route to Europe; families borrow or sell land. A Tarapasha (Derai) villager said half the total contract money must be paid to the broker up front and the rest when the 'game' (sea crossing) is ready. One family in Dowarabazar paid BDT 14 lakh.

According to Jagannathpur residents, local brokers have formed a ring that lures young men with promises of Europe; the young men then pressure their families, who send them by the illegal route either willingly or under pressure.

Azizul Islam of Ichhgaon, Raniganj union, Jagannathpur, Sunamganj is named by families as the broker who took Shayek Ahmad and four other Jagannathpur men who died to Libya to send them to Greece; locals say he is in Libya. A survivor said eight of Azizul's people were on the boat and five of them died.
facts.source_in_article: victims' families, locals and a survivor

facts.statement: Three more brokers of the Jagannathpur area were named by Shayek Ahmad's family and local residents: Shahin Mia of Paragaon village, Enam Ahmad of Balikandi and Karim Mia of Chhilaura village.

facts.statement: Three of the six dead from Derai upazila were from Tarapasha village, Kulanj union; villagers said they went to Libya through a broker named Jasim Uddin of Dowarabazar upazila, who has several local representatives whom people would not name.

Fahim Ahmad (20) of Kabirnagar village, Bogla Bazar union, Dowarabazar died on the boat; locals say his maternal uncle Jamal Uddin sends people to Greece via Libya and Jamal's brother Abdur Rahim alias Jasim Uddin is in Libya. The two brothers are reported to have a case against them in the Human Trafficking Offences Tribunal in Sunamganj. Jamal Uddin did not answer the reporter's phone call.

Sunamganj superintendent of police A B M Zakir Hossain said police are listing brokers from the affected families and confidential information, cases are being prepared at Jagannathpur and Derai police stations, and if no family files a case police will file one themselves, within a day or two.

summary_en: Oman's labour minister assured expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul, at a meeting on 27 January 2026 on the sidelines of the Global Labour Market Conference in Riyadh, that work visas for Bangladeshis would be reopened within two months. headline_en: 309 Bangladeshis return from Libya
summary_en: 309 Bangladeshis who were staying irregularly in Libya returned to Dhaka on Friday 24 October 2025 on a special charter flight arranged with IOM and the Bangladesh embassy in Tripoli. Most had been lured with false promises of reaching Europe across the Mediterranean and many were kidnapped and tortured in Libya. IOM gave each returnee a travel allowance, food and first aid on arrival.

facts.statement: 309 Bangladeshis staying irregularly in Libya were repatriated on a special Fly Oya International charter flight (printed 'ফ্লাই ওয়া ইন্টারন্যাশনাল') with the help of IOM and the Bangladesh embassy in Tripoli, landing at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport at 9 am on Friday 24 October 2025.

Officials of the foreign ministry, the expatriates' welfare ministry and IOM received the returnees from Libya at Dhaka airport; IOM gave each returnee a travel allowance, food items and first aid on arrival.

Most of the 309 returnees had been lured by false promises of being taken to Europe across the Mediterranean and entered Libya illegally through human traffickers; many were later kidnapped and tortured by trafficking networks and armed groups in Libya.

Work is under way by the Bangladesh government, the Bangladesh embassy in Libya, IOM and international partners to repatriate Bangladeshis held in various detention centres in Libya; officials said they are trying to increase coordination with Libyan authorities to stop trafficking and provide safe, legal routes for work abroad.
The returnees from Libya were urged to tell others about their experience to raise awareness of the dangers of irregular migration and human trafficking.

headline_en: Emphasis on skilled labour markets such as Europe and Japan
summary_en: A review of the interim government's first year in the migration sector (August 2025): worker departures have fallen for two years while remittance hit a record of over USD 30 billion in FY2024-25, and the government is pushing skilled markets such as Japan and Europe. It lists which markets are closed (UAE, Oman, Malaysia since June 2024), agreements signed or pending (Italy, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, Iraq and others), protection and service steps abroad and at Dhaka airport, training changes, the replacement of a private registration app with a government platform for emigration clearance, and aid to expatriates freed from UAE and Saudi jails.

facts.statement: As of August 2025, sending workers to the UAE, Bangladesh's second-largest labour market, is stopped; Oman's market is also closed; and Malaysia's labour market has been closed since June 2024. Talks are under way with these countries to reopen quickly. Demand for unskilled workers in Saudi Arabia, the largest market, has fallen.

A migration memorandum of understanding for sending workers has been signed between Bangladesh and Italy; agreements with several more European countries are to follow. Training centres for Italian and Japanese language are being increased in Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare Ministry sources / ministry report

facts.statement: A new agreement has been signed with Japan. The article first says a target has been set to send 1 lakh workers to Japan in the next five years, and later, citing the ministry's report, says a Japan Cell has been formed to send more than 5 lakh workers to Japan in the next five years; the two figures differ in the article.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare Ministry sources; ministry one-year report

facts.statement: Skills tests for sending workers to Japan were previously held in three sectors and have been raised to five sectors; three separate MoUs on skilled-worker training and certification were signed with three Japanese organisations.

An MoU was signed with one province of South Korea to send seasonal workers and sending has begun; two more MoUs are being signed. Demand in Japan and South Korea is far higher than the number of workers Bangladesh is sending.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare Ministry one-year report; reporter

facts.statement: About 15,000 workers who had completed all procedures could not go when Malaysia's labour market closed in 2024. The ministry's report says an agreement has been signed with Malaysia to send 8,000 workers in the initial phase, to be handled by the state agency BOESL at nominal cost, and that after top-level bilateral talks a process has been started to open the Malaysian market to new workers.
Multiple-entry visas have been introduced for Bangladeshi workers in Malaysia for the first time, the ministry's report says.

Bangladesh is due to sign an agreement with Saudi Arabia for the first time in September 2025 to expand safe and legal migration; a joint task force has been formed to resolve the problems of expatriates in Saudi Arabia.
The government has moved to send workers to Iraq, a closed market; a high-level Iraqi delegation is due to visit Bangladesh in September 2025 to sign an MoU.
The attestation process has been withdrawn for Singapore in order to send people there quickly.
Sending doctors and nurses to Guyana (printed 'গায়েনা') is in process; MoUs with Oman, Serbia, Spain, Austria, Malta and Mauritius are at the final stage.
Bangladesh has appointed legal consultancy firms in Qatar, Oman, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Kuwait for its migrant workers, the ministry's report says.

Steps have been taken to regularise irregular Bangladeshi women workers in Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Oman; a process is under way to legalise women workers in Jordan and more than one lakh undocumented workers in Oman.
A 'Probashi Lounge and Waiting Lounge' has been set up at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, with hygienic food available at a 30 percent discount. A hospital for expatriates is planned.

Japanese, English, Chinese and Korean language courses are being run at 44 technical training centres (TTCs). Under an agreement between BMET and the Saudi company Takamol, 15 TTCs and BRTC training centres gained the capacity to run skills tests in the past year. Caregiver training, previously not available at TTCs, has been added.

The previous government had allowed a private company to run a mobile app service for workers' online registration; the interim government shut the private app and built an integrated online platform for overseas employment, and emigration clearance is now issued directly on the government's own digital platform.
facts.source_in_article: reporter / ministry; Tasneem Siddiqui of RMMRU

facts.statement: BMET data: more than 11 lakh workers went abroad in 2022, 13 lakh in 2023, 10 lakh in 2024, and 585,000 in the first seven months of 2025.
Remittance of more than USD 30 billion came to Bangladesh in FY2024-25, the highest in the country's history and 24 percent more than the year before.

The state agency Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) sent 16,066 workers to various countries in FY2024-25, 4 percent more than the previous year; the article describes government-managed sending as cost-free.
The article states that a worker can earn three to four times in Japan or European countries what a worker gets on average per month in the Middle East.

Bangladeshi expatriates who demonstrated abroad in support of the 2024 uprising were detained and sentenced in the UAE; at the chief adviser's request the UAE pardoned them. 188 people from the UAE and 12 from Saudi Arabia were freed and returned home.

The Expatriates' Welfare Ministry gave each of the 188 workers returned from UAE jails BDT 50,000 (BDT 94 lakh in total) plus BDT 13,500 each as counselling and financial incentive. Those who want to go abroad again are to be sent to Brunei; Probashi Kallyan Bank gave rehabilitation loans totalling BDT 86 lakh to 14 applicants, with 12 more in process.

Tasneem Siddiqui, acting executive director of RMMRU, said the government did not allow a syndicate to form for sending workers to Malaysia despite pressure and shut the private registration app, both positive; but the shrinking labour market is a concern and more stress is needed on market expansion and training.

People in the migration sector say that in the past many workers sent abroad found no work, became undocumented, were detained by police and returned, and that rings operating around unskilled recruitment cheated many workers who had paid large sums.

named_actors.what_the_article_says: Saudi company with an agreement with BMET under which 15 TTCs and BRTC training centres can conduct skills tests.

named_actors.what_the_article_says: State agency; sent 16,066 workers in FY2024-25 and is to send the first 8,000 workers to Malaysia at nominal cost.

headline_en: Investigate the allegation of militant activity
summary_en: An editorial on Malaysia's detention of 36 Bangladeshi nationals over alleged militant links. Malaysia's police chief said a ring of Bangladeshi workers spread Islamic State ideology and raised funds among workers through social media; Bangladesh's foreign adviser said the detainees are being sent back and three have already returned and are being questioned. The editorial calls for a proper investigation, warns the affair could hurt worker sending to Malaysia, and says innocent people must not be harassed.

facts.statement: Malaysia's police chief Khalid Ismail told a press conference in Kuala Lumpur on Friday (about 4 July 2025) that 36 Bangladeshi nationals had been detained over alleged militant links; according to Reuters, he said the authorities broke up a ring of Bangladeshi workers that spread Islamic State (IS) ideology among workers and raised funds using social media and online messaging platforms, recruiting other Bangladeshi workers.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian police chief Khalid Ismail, via Reuters, cited in the editorial

facts.statement: Foreign adviser Md. Touhid Hossain said on Thursday (about 3 July 2025) that Bangladeshis detained in Malaysia over alleged involvement in extremist ideology and terrorist activity are being sent back; adviser Asif Nazrul said on Friday night (about 4 July 2025) that three had already returned to Bangladesh and were being questioned.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Touhid Hossain, foreign adviser; Asif Nazrul, law and expatriates' welfare adviser

facts.statement: The editorial warns that the militancy allegation against 36 Bangladeshis could have a negative effect on sending workers to Malaysia, one of Bangladesh's main labour markets, and says the government must investigate credibly while making sure no innocent person is harassed.

named_actors.name: Khalid Ismail
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Malaysia's police chief; announced the detention of 36 Bangladeshis over alleged IS links.

key_quote_bn: শুক্রবার কুয়ালালামপুরে সংবাদ সম্মেলনে মালয়েশিয়ার পুলিশপ্রধান খালিদ ইসমাইল জঙ্গি-সংশ্লিষ্টতার অভিযোগে ৩৬ জন বাংলাদেশি নাগরিককে আটক করার কথা জানান।

headline_en: Bangladeshi young man dies in cylinder explosion in Libya; mourning at his Sirajganj home
summary_en: Nazmul Hossain (25) of Raiganj, Sirajganj, who entered Libya on a tourist visa through a broker in mid-2023 after spending about 5 lakh taka, was burned in a gas cylinder explosion while cooking and died in a hospital there; the family got the news early on Friday 20 June 2025. The family is struggling to bring his body home and locals have asked the authorities to help; the UNO said the matter would be looked into.

facts.statement: Nazmul Hossain (25) of Betua Dakshinpara, Dhangara union, Raiganj upazila, Sirajganj was burned in a gas cylinder explosion while cooking in Libya and died under treatment in a hospital there; the family received the news at dawn on Friday 20 June 2025. He last spoke to his wife on Thursday 19 June 2025. He leaves parents, a sister, a wife and a two-year-old son.
Nazmul Hossain of Sirajganj entered Libya on a tourist visa through a broker in mid-2023 after spending about 5 lakh taka; his mother said the money was borrowed.

Nazmul Hossain's family in Sirajganj is struggling to bring his body back from Libya and a local teacher asked the authorities for help; Raiganj UNO Humayun Kabir said he would inquire and look into the matter. The article records no arrangement for repatriating the body.
facts.source_in_article: local teacher Bidyut Kumar Modak; UNO Humayun Kabir

facts.statement: Local teacher Bidyut Kumar Modak of Raiganj, Sirajganj said many local residents get into danger by going abroad to work on tourist visas, knowingly or unknowingly, and that such incidents happen most in Libya.

people_cases.what_happened: Went in mid-2023 on the advice of acquaintances and relatives, completing the arrangements in secret; burned in a gas cylinder explosion while cooking.
people_cases.outcome: Died in a hospital in Libya (news received 20 June 2025); family seeking help to bring the body home.

headline_en: Who is the kafeel, and why do migrant workers depend on the kafeel
summary_en: An explainer for young readers (Kishor Alo) on the word 'kafeel' and the kafala system in the Middle East: the kafeel is the employer or sponsor who controls a worker's visa and residence permit as well as the job. It describes harsh working conditions, workers' fear of the kafeel, and advises trade training, basic Arabic and understanding the contract and labour law before going. Information support is credited to Shariful Hasan.

facts.statement: In the Middle East a 'kafeel' means the employer or sponsor under whom a person works; under the kafala system the kafeel is not only the worker's employer but also looks after the worker's visa, residence permit and all related matters.
facts.source_in_article: Kishor Alo explainer (information support: Shariful Hasan)

facts.statement: Under the kafala system a worker can lose the job if the kafeel wishes, workers who protest may be threatened with being sent home, and the kafeel's permission is needed even for a sick worker or a dead body to be sent home, the explainer says.

The explainer says a group of people close to kafeels has grown up in the Middle East who exploit workers on the owners' behalf: they supply new workers to factories and use their good relations with owners to deprive ordinary workers of their rights.

The explainer says Bangladeshi workers in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain often work 12 to 14 hours a day in temperatures of 45 to 50 degrees Celsius with little chance to rest; some get good employers but most face cheating, beatings and neglect.
Reform of the kafala (kafeel) system has been under discussion for the past few years, the explainer says, without giving details.

Advice given: before going to the Middle East take trade training such as electrician, plumber, driving or cooking; basic spoken Arabic makes it easier to get work and lowers the cost and the chance of being cheated; workers should have the employment contract properly explained and get an idea of the labour law before leaving.

key_quote_bn: একজন কফিল একজন শ্রমিকের শুধু নিয়োগকর্তা নন ওই শ্রমিকের ভিসা, থাকার অনুমোদন বা রেসিডেন্স পারমিট থেকে শুরু করে সার্বিক বিষয়ে দেখভাল করেন।

headline_en: Stress must be put on stopping illegal migration
summary_en: An editorial welcoming the 'Migration and Mobility' memorandum of understanding recently signed between Italy and Bangladesh to curb illegal migration and expand legal migration. It notes that over 2 lakh Bangladeshis live in Italy, that 60,000 passports were reported stuck in Italy, that MoUs have been signed with six European countries including Portugal and Austria, and that the UAE has announced a limited number of visit visas. It describes how broker rings use visit, student and tourist visas for Romania and eastern Europe, cites Frontex figures, and demands punishment of brokers.

facts.statement: Italy and Bangladesh recently signed a memorandum of understanding on 'Migration and Mobility' aimed at stopping illegal migration and increasing legal migration; the editorial says it will make it easier to send Bangladeshi workers legally according to Italy's demand. Adviser Asif Nazrul and Italian interior minister Matteo Piantedosi spoke at the signing.
There are more than 2 lakh Bangladeshi migrants in Italy, part of whom did not go with valid papers, the editorial says.

In November 2024 foreign adviser Md. Touhid Hossain said 60,000 passports were stuck in Italy, and that if Bangladesh cannot stop illegal migration it will not get opportunities for legal migration to the UK and Europe.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Touhid Hossain, foreign adviser, quoted in the editorial

facts.statement: MoUs have already been signed with six European countries including Portugal and Austria with the aim of increasing legal migration to Europe, the editorial says.
The UAE has announced that it will open a limited number of visit visas for Bangladeshi nationals, the editorial says.
Adviser Asif Nazrul discussed sending skilled women and men workers from Bangladesh during a recent visit to Saudi Arabia.
A class of brokers lures Bangladeshis with promises of high-paid jobs and takes them abroad on visit visas; if caught they are forced to return or must live in hiding there.

A ring of brokers arranges student, tourist and visiting visas for Romania and other eastern European countries, known as 'stepping stones' into Europe, in exchange for large sums; aspirants contact the ring on the word of acquaintances or relatives already staying irregularly in Europe. At least 8 percent of aspirants who later returned home confirmed the ring's existence.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial (source of the 8 percent figure not named)

facts.statement: According to the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex), 55,218 Bangladeshis entered Europe irregularly by various routes between 2014 and 2021.

The editorial says some manpower-exporting firms send workers by illegal routes, and for this reason Bangladesh is on a 'dangerous visa list' for Italy and many other labour-importing countries, and many countries label Bangladesh high-risk.

key_quote_bn: একশ্রেণির দালাল মোটা বেতনের চাকরির প্রলোভন দেখিয়ে তাঁদের বিদেশে নিয়ে যান ভ্রমণ ভিসায়। এ অবস্থায় ধরা পড়লে তাঁরা ফিরে আসতে বাধ্য হন অথবা সেখানে পালিয়ে থাকতে হয়।

headline_en: Expatriates sent record remittance; what will the state give them
summary_en: A column by banker M M Mahbub Hasan sets out figures on the number of Bangladeshis abroad, worker departures and skill levels in 2024, and record remittance (about USD 329 crore in March 2025). It then lists what the state should do for expatriates: curb hundi, train skilled workers, act fast on abuse and contract fraud, treat expatriates properly at the airport, introduce state insurance, raise the remittance incentive from 2.5 to 3.5 percent, and ease passport and ID services. These are proposals, not decisions.

facts.statement: The then expatriates' welfare minister Imran Ahmed told parliament that as of July 2023 the number of Bangladeshi workers employed in various countries was 15,513,460; BMET said the figure was more than 1 crore 48 lakh. The column says the exact number of Bangladeshi expatriates is still not known.
facts.source_in_article: Imran Ahmed in parliament; BMET; cited by the writer

facts.statement: The column states that about 28 lakh Bangladeshi expatriates live in Middle East countries, more than 21 lakh of them in Saudi Arabia, and that Bangladesh ranks after India and Pakistan among foreign workforces in Saudi Arabia. It says 70 to 80 percent of Bangladeshi expatriates live in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait, Oman, Malaysia, the UK, the US and Canada.

According to the column, most Bangladeshi expatriates work as technicians, in domestic work, construction and agriculture; many also work in restaurants, supershops, driving and self-employment, and there are many engineers and doctors.
In FY2022-23 BMET sent a record of about 1,125,833 workers abroad, the highest in 48 years, the column says.
A report by the digital migration platform 'Ami Probashi' said Bangladesh's manpower export fell 27.4 percent in 2024 compared with 2023.
facts.source_in_article: Ami Probashi report, cited by the writer

facts.statement: RMMRU reported that 1,011,959 Bangladeshi workers went abroad in 2024; of them 214,044 were skilled (given as about 23.62 percent) and 491,480 went as low-skilled or unskilled (given as 54.23 percent).
facts.source_in_article: RMMRU report, cited by the writer

facts.statement: Bangladeshi expatriates sent about USD 2,700 crore (27 billion) in remittance in 2024, making Bangladesh seventh in the world and fifth in Asia among remittance-receiving countries; India was top with an estimated USD 12,910 crore.

Remittance to Bangladesh was about USD 329 crore in March 2025 ahead of Eid, a new monthly record; February 2025 brought USD 252 crore, itself the previous single-month record. Remittance over the past 10 years totalled about USD 17,759 crore, and it has risen sharply since the July 2024 uprising.
According to the World Bank, remittance contributes 6 to 7 percent of Bangladesh's national economy.
facts.source_in_article: World Bank, cited by the writer

facts.statement: A 2.5 percent incentive is in force on remittance sent through banking channels; the writer proposes raising it to 3.5 percent and using part of it for life and health insurance cover for the expatriate's family.

The current government has built a VIP lounge inside the airport for expatriates, which the writer says has been widely praised; the writer adds that most expatriates complain they are not treated properly at the airport, sometimes lose valuables and face needless harassment.

The writer says many expatriates send money through hundi instead of banks; technical training centres (TTCs) exist but have not made the desired progress; and proposes zero tolerance for fraud over contracts or wages, fast embassy action on abuse of workers, state insurance for expatriates, easier passport issue and renewal with digital update of data and photo, digital verification and issue of NID, birth registration and other certificates, easy-term loans for expatriate investors, and sending workers to Europe, Japan, South Korea and Australia.

key_quote_bn: ব‍্যাংকিং চ‍্যানেলে প্রবাসী আয় পাঠানোর জন্য বাস্তবায়িত ২ দশমিক ৫ শতাংশ প্রণোদনাকে বাড়িয়ে ৩ দশমিক ৫ শতাংশ করা যেতে পারে।

headline_en: Why women domestic workers who go to Saudi Arabia are coming back as corpses
summary_en: An abridged translation of a New York Times investigation into abuse and deaths of women domestic workers from Kenya and Uganda in Saudi Arabia; it contains nothing about Bangladeshi workers, but it reports Saudi-side rules and practices that apply to foreign domestic workers generally. It records the Saudi human resources ministry's stated protections (10-hour day, weekly day off, online wage payment, complaint channels, repatriation at the employer's or government's cost), and workers' accounts that in practice they are made to pay to go home, are held in shelters run by Sakan and later Samasco, and that deaths with signs of violence are recorded as natural. It also shows politicians in Kenya and Uganda and Saudi royals owning or investing in the recruitment firms.

facts.statement: Saudi human resources ministry spokesperson Mike Goldstein said the Saudi government has raised fines in abuse cases, made it easier for workers to leave a job, limited working time to 10 hours a day, provided for one day off a week, and arranged for domestic workers' wages to be paid online.
facts.source_in_article: Mike Goldstein, spokesperson, Saudi Ministry of Human Resources, to the New York Times

facts.statement: According to the Saudi human resources ministry spokesperson, workers in Saudi Arabia can report abuse, unpaid wages or contract violations through several channels: a hotline, a digital platform and in-person complaint submission. The article does not print the hotline number or platform name.
facts.source_in_article: Mike Goldstein, Saudi Ministry of Human Resources

facts.statement: Under Saudi labour law, when a worker needs to return to their home country the cost must be borne by the employer or the Saudi government; the ministry spokesperson said 'under no circumstances will a worker bear financial responsibility for repatriation'.
facts.source_in_article: Saudi labour law as reported; Mike Goldstein

facts.statement: Returned workers and labour rights groups say that in practice workers in Saudi Arabia are forced to pay their own way home and those who cannot pay are sometimes held; because the visa is tied to the job, those who leave a job risk losing legal status.
facts.source_in_article: returned workers and rights groups, via the New York Times

facts.statement: The Saudi government tasked a company called Sakan with providing housing and legal help to foreign workers in difficulty; the ministry spokesperson said the government stopped funding Sakan in 2023 and a company called Samasco now does this job.

The family of Kenyan worker Hannah Njeri Miriam, in a Sakan-run shelter in 2022, was told she could go home if USD 300 travel cost was paid; three Kenyan women in a Samasco shelter told the New York Times they would not be allowed home unless they paid USD 400 each. Samasco did not respond.
facts.source_in_article: workers and families, via the New York Times

facts.statement: At least 274 Kenyan workers, mostly women, died in Saudi Arabia in the past five years, 55 of them in 2024, double the previous year; autopsy reports are vague and contradictory and deaths are recorded as natural. Uganda has not published its figure.

Ugandan domestic worker Aisha Meeme died in Saudi Arabia; the Saudi autopsy found she was emaciated, with extensive injuries, three broken ribs and severe electrical burn marks on her ear, hands and feet, yet the authorities declared it a natural death. Her husband said the employer offered him a choice between getting her body back or her USD 2,800 in unpaid wages.
facts.source_in_article: husband Isiko Moses Waiswa and autopsy report, via the New York Times

facts.statement: Abuses reported by Kenyan and Ugandan domestic workers in Saudi Arabia include employers holding passports, withholding wages and food, beatings, confinement, rape, and being told to return to work by police and doctors after reporting abuse; one worker who became pregnant after rape by her employer's husband was put on a flight home.
facts.source_in_article: workers interviewed by the New York Times

facts.statement: Ugandan worker Farida Nassanga went to Saudi Arabia as a domestic worker for a wage of USD 200 a month through Marphie International Recruitment Agency.
facts.source_in_article: Farida Nassanga, via the New York Times

facts.statement: The New York Times found that members of the Saudi royal family are major investors in firms that recruit domestic workers, and politicians and their families in Kenya and Uganda own the firms that send workers; some companies' websites show women workers with an 'add to cart' option.

By Saudi government figures, about 5 lakh (half a million) workers from Kenya and Uganda work in Saudi Arabia, most of them women working as domestic workers. Documents show Kenya and Uganda did not get the worker-safety guarantees that many other countries obtain from Saudi Arabia before sending workers.
facts.source_in_article: Saudi government figures; New York Times review of documents

facts.statement: Milton Turyasiima, assistant commissioner at Uganda's Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development, said abuse in Saudi Arabia is still widespread and complaints arrive every day.

named_actors.what_the_article_says: Company that took over the shelter role from Sakan; three Kenyan women said they were asked for USD 400 each to be allowed home.

named_actors.name: Fabian Kyule Muli
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Vice chairman of the Kenyan parliament's labour committee who also owns a firm sending women workers to Saudi Arabia; a worker sent by it was told she could 'swim across the Red Sea' home.

Phoned home in 2022 saying her employer threatened to kill her and had thrown her into a water tank.

people_cases.what_happened: Died with injuries, broken ribs and electrical burns per the autopsy.
people_cases.outcome: Declared a natural death; husband offered either the body or USD 2,800 unpaid wages.

people_cases.what_happened: Went in 2019 on USD 200 a month; raped and beaten by her employer's husband, became pregnant.
people_cases.outcome: Put on a flight to Uganda; seeking compensation with legal aid; agency's Saudi partner did not respond.

people_cases.what_happened: Beaten by the employer's children, wages withheld, locked on a third-floor roof without food or water; jumped and injured her spine; police and doctor told her to go back to work.
people_cases.outcome: Sent home by the Saudi placement agency in 2023; cannot work because of chronic pain.

people_cases.paid: USD 300 demanded for travel; not paid
people_cases.what_happened: Dismissed by employer in 2022 and stayed in a Sakan shelter where she said she was mistreated.
people_cases.outcome: Died; family told she fell from the second floor trying to escape; autopsy said head injury, police said heart and respiratory failure.

people_cases.what_happened: Sexually harassed and abused by her employer; phoned the recruiting firm for help.
people_cases.outcome: Died; Kenyan government attributed death to a 'nerve problem'.

key_quote_bn: সৌদি আরবের শ্রম আইন অনুযায়ী, যখন একজন শ্রমিকের নিজ দেশে ফেরার প্রয়োজন হবে, তখন সেটার ব্যয়ভার নিয়োগকারী বা সৌদি সরকারকে বহন করতে হবে।
